abstract: Cerebrovascular health has emerged as a crucial factor in influencing cognitive decline in aging, including cognitive control and fluid intelligence. Previous studies have largely relied on peripheral assessments of vascular health due to the paucity of global and regional estimates of cerebrovascular status. This study uses the pulse relaxation function (PReFx), a measure of pulse-wave shape based on diffuse optical tomography (pulse-DOT), to provide regional estimates of arterial elasticity in the cortical mantle. For the first time, we integrate a network-based approach based on previous fMRI studies and pulse-DOT regional mapping of cerebrovascular status, to test whether the support provided by the cerebrovascular system to different brain networks may differentially impact cognitive control performance. To comprehensively assess how various mechanisms of cognitive control are influenced by the cerebrovascular health of different networks, we used a task-switching paradigm that simultaneously measures proactive and reactive control processes. After removing the global signal, we found that larger positive PReFx residual values in the Dorsal Attention and Visual Networks are linked to lower cognitive control costs. Conversely, larger positive residual values in the Default Mode and Fronto-Parietal Networks are associated with higher cognitive control costs. These results indicate that the relative balance of arterial elasticity across different brain networks impacts cognitive control, highlighting the importance of studying network-based cerebrovascular status for understanding cognitive performance.
